models.name: Gaussian Process Regression (GPR)
models.description: A probabilistic surrogate that models the output as a sample from a Gaussian Process. Provides a full posterior distribution — not just a point prediction but also a confidence interval around it. Four kernels are available: RBF (default, infinitely smooth), Matérn ν=2.5 (twice differentiable), Matérn ν=1.5 (once differentiable, suits rough surfaces), and Rational Quadratic (mixture of length scales). All kernels use ARD — one length scale per input — so the model automatically down-weights irrelevant inputs during training.
strengths: Native uncertainty estimates (posterior std) at every prediction point
Four kernel choices (RBF, Matérn 2.5, Matérn 1.5, Rational Quadratic) span smooth to rough responses
ARD length scales expose relative input importance in the Results panel
Well-calibrated confidence intervals when model assumptions hold
weaknesses: Scales as O(n³) in training time — impractical beyond ~2,000 points
Struggles with high-dimensional inputs (> 10–15 variables)
Poor extrapolation — reverts to prior mean outside training range
models.best_for: Smooth to moderately rough, low-dimensional responses (< 15 inputs) with < 2,000 training points where uncertainty quantification is required. Default to RBF; switch to Matérn 2.5 or 1.5 if R² is below 0.90.
models.avoid_when: Dataset has > 2,000 rows, > 15 inputs, or the response has discontinuities.

models.name: Random Forest (RF)
models.description: An ensemble of decision trees, each fitted on a bootstrap sample of the data using a random subset of features. Predictions are averaged across all trees. Extremely robust — handles non-linear, non-smooth responses, categorical features, and high-dimensional inputs without normalisation.
strengths: Handles non-smooth, discontinuous responses naturally
Scales to large datasets (100,000+ rows) efficiently
Robust to irrelevant inputs — unimportant features are rarely selected
Free uncertainty estimate via tree variance (percentile spread across trees)
weaknesses: Does not interpolate exactly — predictions are step-like near training points
Extrapolates poorly — predicts a constant (the mean of nearby leaves) outside training range
Slower to evaluate than linear models for very large forests
models.best_for: Non-smooth responses, large datasets, high-dimensional inputs, or when robustness is more important than smoothness.
models.avoid_when: The response is known to be smooth and small dataset size makes GPR tractable — GPR will usually be more accurate in that case.

models.name: Radial Basis Function (RBF)
models.description: Constructs the surrogate as a weighted sum of radial basis functions centred at each training point. Thin-plate spline (default) and multiquadric kernels are supported. Always passes exactly through training points (exact interpolation). No probabilistic interpretation.
strengths: Fast evaluation — closed-form analytical prediction
Exact interpolation through all training points
No hyperparameters to tune (thin-plate spline has none)
Works well for low-dimensional smooth responses
weaknesses: No uncertainty estimates
Can produce oscillation artifacts between training points in high dimensions or when training points are poorly distributed
Ill-conditioned for large datasets or clustered points
models.best_for: Small, well-distributed datasets with smooth responses where exact interpolation is desired and speed is a priority.
models.avoid_when: Large datasets, clustered samples, high-dimensional inputs, when uncertainty estimates are needed, or when training data contains measurement noise — RBF interpolates exactly through every point including noise artefacts, producing training R²=1.0 that does not reflect true model accuracy.

models.name: Polynomial Chaos Expansion (PCE)
models.description: Represents the surrogate as a multivariate polynomial in the input variables using orthogonal basis functions (Legendre polynomials for uniform inputs). The coefficients encode all information about the response. First-order Sobol sensitivity indices are free byproducts — no separate analysis needed.
strengths: First-order Sobol sensitivity indices (S₁) computed analytically from polynomial coefficients — no additional sampling required
Algebraically interpretable — each coefficient has physical meaning
Fast evaluation — purely polynomial arithmetic
Very accurate for smooth, well-behaved responses
weaknesses: Order 3 expansion has (n+3 choose 3) terms — blows up in high dimensions
Fails completely on non-smooth or discontinuous responses
Assumes inputs are uniformly distributed (or can be mapped to uniform)
models.best_for: Smooth, low-dimensional (< 8 inputs) responses where analytical sensitivity is desired alongside the surrogate.
models.avoid_when: Non-smooth responses, > 10 inputs (curse of dimensionality), or input distributions far from uniform.

models.name: Linear Model (Ridge Regression)
models.description: Fits a linear combination of input variables to the output using Ridge regularisation (L2 penalty) to prevent overfitting. The simplest possible surrogate — linear in every input. Fast, interpretable, and a useful baseline to beat before using more complex models.
strengths: Fastest possible training and prediction
Fully interpretable — each coefficient is a sensitivity
Stable on small datasets due to Ridge regularisation
Useful baseline: if a non-linear model barely beats it, the response may be approximately linear
weaknesses: Cannot model non-linear relationships at all
No uncertainty estimates
Poor on interactions between inputs (would need feature engineering)
models.best_for: Approximately linear responses, or as a fast baseline model before investing in GPR or RF.
models.avoid_when: The response is known to be non-linear — this model will systematically underfit.

models.name: Multi-Fidelity Surrogate
models.description: Combines data from two or more simulation fidelity levels — many cheap low-fidelity (LF) runs for global coverage plus a small number of expensive high-fidelity (HF) runs for local accuracy. Two strategies are available: Bridge Correction trains an LF surrogate on all LF data, then trains a separate correction model on the discrepancy (HF − LF prediction) at HF points; final prediction is LF + correction. Kennedy-O'Hagan Co-Kriging models HF as ρ × f_LF + δ(x) where ρ is a scaling factor and δ is a Gaussian process correction, providing native prediction intervals.
strengths: Achieves HF accuracy at a fraction of the HF simulation cost
LF data provides global coverage; HF data provides local corrections
Bridge Correction is non-parametric — no assumption about LF/HF relationship
Co-Kriging provides full uncertainty estimates propagating both LF and correction uncertainty
weaknesses: Requires two datasets with matching input column names
Degrades if LF and HF outputs are poorly correlated (R² < 0.70 between fidelities)
Co-Kriging is more expensive to train and sensitive to the ρ scaling assumption
Bridge Correction can overfit the correction model if the HF dataset is very small (< 10 points)
models.best_for: Aerospace and structural problems with an existing large LF dataset (CFD/FEA) and a budget for 20–50 HF runs. Most effective when HF simulations are at least 5–10× more expensive than LF.
models.avoid_when: LF and HF outputs are poorly correlated, the LF dataset is smaller than the HF dataset, or the two fidelity levels use different input parameterisations.

models.name: Ensemble Surrogate
models.description: Combines two or more individual surrogate models into a single weighted prediction. Three weighting strategies: equal (1/n), CV-performance (weights proportional to cross-validation R²), and stacking (a Ridge meta-model learns weights from held-out predictions). More robust than any individual model on complex response surfaces.
strengths: More robust than any single model — errors from different models tend to cancel
Gracefully degrades if one component fails — failed components are excluded
Stacking strategy adapts weights to the data rather than assuming equal performance
Free uncertainty proxy — variance across component predictions
weaknesses: Training time = sum of all component training times
Harder to interpret than any single model
May not outperform the best single model if one component is clearly dominant
models.best_for: Complex, multi-modal response surfaces where no single model type dominates. Production surrogates where robustness matters more than interpretability.
models.avoid_when: One model type is clearly the best choice and training time is a constraint.
